utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Before I give you an opportunity to continue, Mr. Tieger, Mr. Josse, we are working hard on next Monday, but it takes an enormous effort. I couldn't tell you whether we'll be successful, but that should become clear somewhere in the next hour. But it takes quite something to reschedule because one of the Chambers could not swap with us because of videolinks already being prepared, and the other one is a very complex case. So therefore I really couldn't tell you whether we are successful, but the mere fact that we are still trying hard should be of some comfort to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Perhaps we could return to that subject later, depending on the news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's do that. Then, Mr. Radojko, I'd like to remind you -- first of all, good afternoon to you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Yes, Mr. Tieger will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, before I begin, we have some updated information about some of the exhibit numbers yesterday. I believe that's been provided to the registrar, but I don't know whether it's helpful or not to actually recite them for the Court at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's not lose ourselves in quoting all kinds of numbers. If we come across in any way any of these exhibits and the numbering of it, we'll deal with it; otherwise, I take it, on the basis of what you found, we'll get new information saying exactly what is what number, perhaps including the numbers assigned to it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. I would only note that I think two of the items received new numbers. They were previous exhibits, and one of the documents refer -- which was introduced yesterday still needs a number. So I just bring that to the attention of the registrar in case we wanted to use one of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, if you would assign a new number that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. P1102 and 1103, which were already assigned numbers, so they would be available, free. P1104, which was the 2nd Krajina Corps Command order on forming prisoner of war camps, dated 25th June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, where do we find that on our list in relation to the tabs?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be tab 33, Your Honours. The description does not show on the index.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see. 1104 is now -- is already on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So P1104 would now be P1102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's tab 33?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 33, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that is now 1102.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And tab 14, which is pending, which we did not give a number yesterday, would be P1103; tab 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. That's the intercept. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radojko.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe we -- I will ask you to return to tab 37, where I think we concluded before we adjourned yesterday. That's the report on the events in Bosanski Petrovac from June 1992. And if I can ask you to look at the reference to July 14th regarding the destruction of the mosque on that date, further reference to destruction of another mosque on September 15th, and then a reference on the subsequent page in English - I'm not sure how it appears on your copy - to the destruction of the mosque in Rasinovac, which had been demolished earlier. As you indicated yesterday, that information is accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that the mosques had been pulled down because the president of the Executive Board had to look for someone to dispose of the remains because some parts of the building were a hazard to passersby.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And it's correct that those mosques were not just damaged but were fully destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the --

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the construction of those mosques? What were they made of?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, afterwards I used to walk by that place, because I used to live in a place which was close by, and as far as I could tell, they were made of some solid material. As to whether it was stone or brick, I don't know. I could see bits of plaster, but at any rate it was pretty hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So would it be correct then that they were blown up with explosives?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is indeed correct to say that, because on one occasion I was awake at night when a powerful explosion took place, and afterwards I heard stories that on that occasion a mosque was destroyed. I'm certain about one occasion like that because everybody was talking about it in town, and I suppose the others met with the same fate. So there were the remains and I could see that one had indeed been destroyed by explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell us who or what group or groups blew up the mosques?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never established who blew up the mosques. I do know that the police used to say that they didn't even have any indication as to who it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you to turn to the second page in English, and that will be a reference -- just a couple of paragraphs beyond the indication of the destruction of the mosque in Rasinovac. And that describes a meeting with Muslim representatives and Mr. Novakovic, along with the complete War Presidency. And it indicates that: "[Mr. Novakovic] told us that we would be able to exchange the houses and that it would be made possible for us to leave Petrovac because there was no way that the Muslims and Serbs could live together in Petrovac any longer." First of all, I want -- if you know, I want you to assist us in setting the date of that meeting. The report is intended to be chronological, as it indicates in its preface, and it proceeds roughly chronologically, but there is a -- that date is not indicated and there is a reference to June 20th afterwards. We see that on July 14th the mosque in Srednji Biscani was blown up, and that seems to be an occasion in the report to indicate the destruction of the mosques earlier and later. And then the next paragraphs indicate: "We got a message from Safet Hidic," and it proceeds to discuss that and says: "We got a message from Safet Hidic and Ejub Topic from the meeting with the Serbian authorities in Korenica in late June ..." And then it says: "We were received by the mayor, Mr. Novakovic, along with the complete War Presidency." And the next reference is then to an exchange of houses with the Serbs from Bihac started -- I'm sorry, excuse me, the next reference is: "The first contact with UNPROFOR was made in Lapac on July 16th, 1992 ..." And finally, this may be helpful after the reference to Mr. Novakovic's meeting with the Muslim delegation: "They set up a commission for the contact with the Muslims, headed by Obrad Vrzina." Does that assist you in setting a more precise date for that meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it difficult to remember the date, but I can reconstruct the part of all this. This meeting with the Serb authorities at Korenica, well, they said that they got a message from Safet Hidic and Ejub Topic. This Topic person is somebody I don't know from Petrovac, so I suppose it must be one of the Muslim leaders from Bihac, because at that stage Safet Hidic had already gone to Bihac, and I suppose that it must have been there that they sent a message, either through UNPROFOR or somebody else, I do not know, because Muslims from that delegation that I was a part of as well wanted to have separate talks with the UNPROFOR representatives, so they did. And I suppose this information was obtained in the course of that conversation, I don't know, because I was left in an adjoining room on my own. But here the reference is to Husein Odobasic's delegation --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, I apologise for that, and perhaps you're thinking out loud, trying to reconstruct the dates by reciting the events, but if you can assist us with the date, that would be appreciated; if not, I'm not seeking at this moment the precise substance of each and every one of those meetings. Did that meeting take place right around the time of the establishment of the commission which was headed by Mr. Vrzina?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to this meeting and this make-up of the Muslim delegation and the Serb delegation, well, I didn't know about it. Presumably this is when the dignitaries from both the Muslim and the Serb side attended some kind of meeting, because this is outside the context at Lapac. They are saying that the meeting was at Korenica, which is quite some way away. And secondly, the second meeting, the fact that they were met by the entire War Presidency, well, I certainly did not attend a meeting of this sort because I was at a meeting prior to the very departure. It was in September, when I was in charge of the minutes -- or rather, I was taking notes. And presumably, presumably, looking at the time, these meetings overlap with the time when Mr. Vrzina was elected to that commission -- yes, it's come to me now. At the time when Obrad Vrzina was appointed the president of the commission, I as a legal expert was also appointed to that commission. I can remember that now. I saw that document at the previous trial. I was in the battle-field and it would have been in July 1992, because I had been mobilised at that time, and when I came back somebody told me by the way that I had been appointed for that commission, but that commission did no work at all. Perhaps Vrzina himself attended some meetings himself, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to put a question to you. In order to come back to this destruction of the mosques, were those isolated incidents or did it fall within the framework of a general trend towards destruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those mosques were pulled down in a period of time which was rather brief. I do not remember whether it went on for a week or a little bit longer or a little bit less, but they had been destroyed. All that happened was in the morning we heard, okay, the mosque had been destroyed. As to the destruction of mosques, later on in 1992, on one occasion in the month of May, or maybe earlier, I was on my way to Banja Luka on some business and I realised that Ferhadija mosque had been destroyed. And I think I must have been there on the day after the event. And it is possible that there were such destructions at the same time in several places, but this is, roughly speaking, the period of time in which that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was very specific: I wanted to know whether those mosques or one of those mosques had been destroyed in the course of some bombing campaigns that could have destroyed houses as well or whether they were individualised as targets and were destroyed as targets, as specific targets.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I had not quite understood your question. On those occasions, the mosques were the only targets. There was no bombing or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the report on the events mentions also, on the second page, that UNPROFOR refused to agree to escort them out for already known reasons. I think you made reference in your testimony earlier, during the examination-in-chief, to the fact that there was no international participation in the convoys that you described at length during your testimony. If I can, I'd like to show you now the next exhibit, and that's a news article dated August 13th, 1992, a Reuters article that needs to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it need a number, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1104, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radojko, I want to direct your attention to a few references in that article and then ask you about them. As you can see, in the first sentence the article states that: "The United Nations has challenged Serb plans to evict 28.000 Muslims from besieged towns in northern Bosnia, and warns Serb forces 'the whole world will know' if refugees are harmed." The third paragraph quotes a spokeswoman for the -- for UNHCR saying: "We have told local authorities that if any harm comes to these people, the whole world will know." Further down the page you'll see the number 20.000. It says: "More than 20.000 people are stranded crossing the Bosnian-Croatian border and thousands more to the south." And the next sentence references the "Serbs' most ambitious 'ethnic cleansing' to date." And the final reference I want to bring your attention to at this moment appears at the first sentence of the English, and that's about three short paragraphs after the reference to Dr. Karadzic in this article. And it says: "Most of the families are Muslim, huddled at the border town of Bosanski Novi, he said. Others are believed to be grouping further south in Bosanski Petrovac." The potential departure of Muslims from Petrovac that were the subject of the reference in the Bosanski Petrovac report during July and August were not an isolated event in Petrovac but were part of a much wider movement of Muslims in the Bosnian Krajina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt because I've had a chance to glance at this document. The witness really needs to read it all, to be given a moment to read it all. I have submissions to make about the document in due course, but I'll wait until the cross-examination on it is finished. But in my submission, selective use of this document in this way is not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure in what respect it's unfair with respect to this particular question, Your Honour. I'm more than happy in any event to have the witness to take as much time to review it as he wishes and requires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, could you please read through the document and tell us when you're finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, and I don't want to make too much of a fuss about this, but if this is some sort of insinuation by counsel that this is an unfair use of this document, I'd like to hear about it more directly and exactly what it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is, Mr. Tieger, that in order to give any decision on that, we would have to read it as well. I mean, only once we have read it or once we hear from Mr. Josse and put it all in context. It would take just as much time as to give the witness an opportunity. The fact that the Chamber gives an opportunity to the witness to read the document is not in any way to be understood as either accepting or not accepting the observations made by Mr. Josse. It's just a practical solution for the present situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm content with that at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've read through the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you recall the question, Mr. Radojko, and can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. I'm not familiar with these other events, apart the reference to Petrovac at the time. Here it says it is presumed that more refugees are being gathered south of Petrovac. It's the 13th of August, 1992. Back then, there was a huge influx of Serb refugees into Petrovac, and up until September, October, about 6.000 of them arrived at Petrovac. And Muslims simply lived in their own houses. They were not gathered anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask you two questions then and I'll break them down. First of all, are you saying that you had no idea that outside of Petrovac Muslims were leaving, in whatever way, in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I meant, and I didn't actually put it like that. I started saying that I was familiar with some instances of them leaving because when we left with the first convoy and when we were threatened and they threatened us and said that we would be killed, and on that occasion we were told that others had already gone through from the municipalities of Sanski Most and Kljuc. And then on the day on which we were meant to leave, we asked from the Kljuc municipality to send us some buses. And they promised to do so, but on that day the buses did not get there. And when we encountered problems, security-related problems, in crossing Vlasic, and on that occasion we were told that the Kljuc people had been there in their own convoy. And that's why, apparently, there were not enough soldiers to escort us and that's why we had difficulties. So on at least two occasions I knew for a fact that there had been people moving out from other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The second question is: Did you understand from the representatives of the international community that their unwillingness to participate in the departure of Muslims from Petrovac was due to their understanding or allegations that Muslims were being forced out of municipalities around the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their claim is a general one here. Perhaps it applies to some places, but I can claim that it is not correct in relation to Petrovac. Would you list property and real estate, seal that property, create security and all that, and take care of these people if we had been after ethnic cleansing? I mean, there were also agreements amongst people in order to have Serbs keep an eye on their property, et cetera. And I think all these indications point to the contrary. I can't talk about any other situation any other place, because all I know about those is rumours, so of course anything is possible. But in the case of Petrovac I know that everybody worked on the assumption that the Muslims would be back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My question was, Mr. Radojko, whether you understood at that time, in the summer of 1992, that the international community was refusing to participate in these convoys, this movement of Muslims, because they believed it to be ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that they said explicitly that they believed that it might be ethnic cleansing, and that's why they would not provide any assistance in those people being transferred to Split. That was the delegation that included Druzic, Odobasic, myself, I don't know whether Gacesa was there at the time, I can't remember. On that occasion, that's what we were told. And we didn't go only once. But on the occasion of the second or the third meeting, we were told that they wouldn't play any part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I noted that you distinguished to some extent Petrovac from other municipalities. And if I recall correctly, you made such a distinction during the course of your testimony in the Brdjanin case as well.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at 20359 you were asked: "Now, finally, and this is how matters began yesterday, when you were cross-examined by Mr. Cunningham. He put to you something you had said in an interview, at the end, I believe it was, that you believed that the authorities in Bosanski Petrovac - this is page 37 of yesterday's LiveNote - did whatever was possible. 'The essential goal --'" the Prosecutor is quoting your testimony. "'The essential goal, the essential intention, was for people to be removed from danger, and unfortunately, if you look at it from the outside, we seem exactly the same, in a way, as the municipalities that organised the persecution of their population and organised their removal.' "The first question is: Which municipalities are you thinking of?" And you responded: "It's difficult to name individual municipalities, but in the press, I read on various occasions, especially after the war, and up to an extent in the wartime press, written, printed written by refugees. For instance, a paper published by Muslims, refugees from Sanski Most. And they explicitly said there that they had been rounded up and forced out, forced to become refugees. I also learnt about the municipality of Banja Luka, that there were such round-ups. I could see on Belgrade television, and I could hear people make statements how they had been rounded up and how they had even to pay to be allowed to leave and considerable amounts at that. So these are municipalities that I meant, for instance, and you can find a lot of it in the press." Now, just to round this out, I'll attempt to paraphrase as accurately as possible. If a more accurate reading is required, I'll be pleased to do so. You were then asked about your contact with the municipality of Prijedor. You said these contacts happened twice, and you described them in full. "The president may have communicated more often, but not at the time when Stakic became the president of the Serb Democratic Party for the subregion --"

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, that was in response to a question as to whether he had any other contact with that municipality, and the answer was: "No." And then he went on to say: "These contacts that existed happened twice ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then after the passage I quoted, you were asked: "All right. Would you describe Prijedor as one of the municipalities that organised the persecution of the population and their removal?" And you said: "Well, on the basis of the information that I found, as I have described, yes, I believe that Prijedor was one of those municipalities, and after all, it is common knowledge as to what went on in Prijedor. Today, on our television, we often see stories about people expelled, I mean taken from their homes, and so on." And then you went on to say but at that time you "didn't know about it because it was all -- nobody spoke about this. There was silence about it. None of the municipal mayors, at least the meeting I was present, you couldn't hear anything about that, even though one heard that Muslims were leaving our municipalities. But simply, whether it was a taboo subject or not, perhaps in those circles, who were rather broad when I was, I mean, present there, so they didn't discuss it, but it was never mentioned. People knew that -- that there were people leaving, but nobody knew exactly how." Now, one of the contacts you had with Mr. Stakic referred to -- well, first of all, let me confirm that that's -- that that information is accurate as you related in the course of the Brdjanin testimony. I mean, is that -- that's what you said at that time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have definitely stated that. However, you've mentioned a whole lot of information that I cannot now confirm individually because there was a great deal of it. But generally speaking, yes, that's what I stated. I mentioned every single contact that I had with whomsoever, and I have documents corroborating that. I can tell you only that at least at a later stage I found out what had been going on earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I wanted to take you to those specific contacts. The first contact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to your municipality, sir, and I'm referring to your municipality only, was the departure of those Muslims voluntary or not? In trying to determine that, I would like to put the following question to you: Do you recognise that the living conditions for those Muslims back then in your town and around your town were such as to basically leave them no choice but to leave? Do you believe that their living conditions, their circumstances at the time, led them to volunteer to leave? Let me clarify this. If they were bombed, threatened, victimised non-stop, they of course would have volunteered to leave. Do you allow that, I don't know who, but somebody, ensured that their circumstances were such as to lead them to wish to leave your municipality and go to live somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already answered the question, and I will repeat: The largest group that departed, regardless of the fact that their representative volunteered to leave, in my opinion, the group did not leave out of their own will because the situation that you described here indicates that they did not wish to leave but rather wished to seek safety. People who left earlier on left of their own will, because at the time the pressure was not that prominent and the local authorities kept the situation under control. However, when the new bodies of authorities were starting to be set up and the JNA started being dissolved, these gangs circulated around, the conditions changed. And under those circumstances, I believe they were compelled to leave, especially during the two or three days when there was general shooting and violence. That was shortly before their departure, I believe two or three days before their departure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But do you mean to say that this pressure which had been brought to bear by these external elements was something that simply escaped any control? Are you going as far as to say that the situation was so chaotic as to make any sort of control of the situation impossible and that whatever happened could not be kept under control or could not be checked in any way? Is that what you're trying to say? That is to say are you saying that neither the civilian nor the military authorities were in a position to bring the situation under control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I'm trying to say. There was general intolerance and resentment. Look at Iraq at present day. Who can put the matters under control? There was general hatred. The society and the communities were separated. The different communities wished to defend their own interests that were conflicting. Over 100 persons were required to keep guard in a small -- stand guard in a small town, and still they could not protect everyone. It bears noting that part of the town was populated by Serbs and the other by Muslims, which meant that it wasn't the whole of the town that they had to protect. The attackers were never quite identified, although I believe that they were Serbs, and those who were standing guard had to open fire at them. So you could hear gun-shots and grenades being thrown everywhere around. And these were people who had only gone through their military service some 10 or 20 years earlier and could barely hold a piece of weapon. That was what the situation was like. And you can see that what I'm saying is the truth because still the situation is such that that indicates that we cannot be together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, I indicated that I was going to direct your attention to the two occasions you asserted that you had contact with Dr. Stakic from Prijedor during summer of 1992. The first occasion was reflected in your diary, and you've testified about that. That was a meeting, a May 12th meeting, with representatives of the army and other municipalities. And at that time, among other things, you sought to obtain fuel from Prijedor, which had a military warehouse. And you made arrangements to get in touch with Dr. Stakic to obtain that fuel, and you did so. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the other occasion also reflected in your diary was a meeting of the 7th of June, a meeting in Sanski Most, and specifically in Palanka, Sanski Most, of the -- entitled: The subregional meeting of seven municipalities, including Petrovac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We did not meet the first time. We had a telephone contact. I didn't know him. I received an order, and I carried it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And it was in connection with the -- of obtaining oil from the military warehouse in Prijedor. That part's accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the second occasion was the 7 June 1992 subregional meeting of seven municipalities?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sent to attend the meeting on behalf of the president. I merely collected the information at the meeting and went back. I did not have a special role there. I recall this event during my earlier testimony because it wasn't that relevant to me. I had to relay a message from some of the commanders, and that was the end of the story. They took notes of the meeting, and I believe that possibly they sent the minutes to Petrovac later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn to tab 26. You'll see the conclusions adopted at the subregional meeting on the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's at -- and that's P529, tab 343, Your Honour; also P192.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Conclusion number 6 from that meeting is that: "All seven municipalities in our subregion agree that Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities until a level is reached where Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented on its own territory in each of these municipalities. In this respect, we request that the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina provide a corridor for the re-settlement of Muslims and Croats to Central Bosnia and Alija's independent state of BH because they voted for it. If the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and Banja Luka fails to solve this issue, our seven municipalities will take all Muslims and Croats under military escort from our municipalities to the centre of Banja Luka." So, Mr. Radojko, that information reflected further information available to you about what was happening and why it was happening to the Muslims and Croats in the adjacent municipalities in the ARK, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no such discussion at this particular meeting. We sat at a desk at this meeting, had a drink, and we agreed that the organiser - that was either the municipality of Krupa or that of Prijedor - that they would draw-up conclusions and disseminate them. And that was the end of the story because the representatives of these municipalities were not even officially there -- or rather, the relevant municipalities were not represented. I must point out that a lot of what is written here is grammatically incorrect, and whoever drafted this must have been writing something that is simply a wish list, because these matters were not discussed at this meeting, because I assure you that I would have taken note of them in my diary and I would have relayed the information to the president. If you talk to the other participants in this meeting, you would be told that none of the matters listed here were in fact discussed. This is nonsensical. These are matters that could not simply be implemented, not even in this way, as written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as you subsequently found out, Mr. Radojko, they were implemented in, essentially, that way, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. The authors of such texts must have implemented them, too. But I assure you that such matters could not have been discussed at this meeting. There were senior officers, military officers, who would not wish to participate in such meetings in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I thought from reading your previous testimony that the reason you didn't take more notes about this meeting is because Mr. Latinovic was there, so there wasn't much need for you to do so.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that Mr. Latinovic was there. But there was no need for that because those who organised the meeting were not there. It was only when my municipality organised the meeting that I took notes, and you can see that. It transpires from my archives. Otherwise, only if something specific needed to be done would I take detailed notes of that. At the time, I didn't know what the contents of some of these messages of the military officers were, but I relayed them all the same. I recall that one piece of information where I was supposed to relay a message saying that somebody need not have been criminally prosecuted for something. I don't really remember, I didn't know what it was all about. Besides, a lot of time was -- this was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Latinovic briefed the Crisis Staff about the conclusions adopted from that meeting on -- just a couple of days later - and if you can turn to the next tab - in fact, just the next day. And that's tab 27, P90, tab 24, which reflect the minutes of the 28th session of the Crisis Staff. And if you'll turn to item number 2, contained on page 2 of the English, it indicates that: "Bogdan Latinovic informed the participants about the conclusions adopted at the meeting that was held at Luska Palanka with the representatives of the seven municipalities."

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, but I assure you that the minutes were not drafted or disseminated at the time because under those circumstances it was impossible for it to take place so soon. To tell you the truth, I don't know anything specific about it. But judging from what -- from the way things were done back then, I can tell you that this wasn't the case. I know that the mood at the meeting was pleasant. They had a drink, I don't know whether they had something to eat as well. I only remember that there was nothing specific for me to do. I was simply sitting there on one side of the desk, and when the meeting finished, I went back. That was the end of it for me. It is quite possible that some of the matters were indeed discussed, but I assure you that none of these were subject of any conclusions. Nothing was concluded on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned during the course of your earlier testimony that Mr. Novakovic had a conversation with Dr. Karadzic after the convoy, and that Dr. Karadzic was angry. You didn't mention that during the course of your Brdjanin testimony, as I recall, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I mentioned it or not. At any rate, whatever I said was truthful. Nobody asked me about any such thing, and nobody put such a question to me here either. I'm trying to simply answer from my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It wouldn't surprise you, I take it, if -- since you think that Dr. Karadzic knew about it from Mr. Novakovic, that the subject of the convoy was well-known and that the other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership knew about that convoy.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know how it was that they made contact on that day, because when we arrived in Knezevo it was night-time already and the army took over and told us to wait there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Wait --

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned the following day --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Radojko, we're -- I want to spare us the time. If you don't know whether or not other people know about that, I want to direct your attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm rising because that wasn't the question that was asked. The question that was asked I, in fact, was waiting for the answer because I was going to object to it. It was pure assumption. The question was put on the basis, "It wouldn't surprise you, would it," rather than the question that has now just been asked quite differently. In my submission, the first question is assumption, the second question is perfectly fair. Perhaps my learned friend could ask a proper question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's move on to another question. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Radojko, that what upset the Bosnian Serb leaders about this convoy is the fact that they were in the course of negotiations with the international community and that more ethnic cleansing put them in a bad negotiating posture. Isn't that right, and didn't you know that at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about this at the time. Today, I can't say what their thoughts were. Your assumption may be right --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in view of the events at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to tab 48, which contain remarks by General Mladic at the 20th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. And let me ask you to look through that for a reference to General Rob and the inhabitants of Petrovac. Let me see if I can be of assistance to you in just a moment. If you'll -- contained on page 21 of the English, and if you'll look through your portion, you'll see a reference to Martic and General Dukic, and then a further reference to Martic and then the quote I want to bring your attention to. And I'll read you the full quote; it may assist you as well. "General Rob was particularly interested in the evacuation of inhabitants of Petrovac and I want to tell you about that. In the past few days the civilian authorities and the Red Cross organised buses, eight on one day and five on the next day. We should be careful about these things, they shouldn't happen prior to meetings and conferences because they undermine the negotiating positions of our leadership. I told them that the Muslims and Croats did this before every conference, and I told him frankly that we give their people buses and take them to Split while they throw our people into pits and never turn them over to anyone." Now, did Mr. Milanovic or Mr. Novakovic indicate to you at any point that that was the source of the irritation by the Bosnian Serb leadership over the timing of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never told me anything about it. This is the first time I hear of it actually discussed this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Radojko, in any event, that by the 28th of October, by late October, there was hardly a Muslim left in Petrovac? And I'm just quoting you from your testimony in Brdjanin at 20210.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for that. It's true; that's correct. There's no need for that. I said so yesterday as well, except for those who remained in one village just outside the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could turn your attention next to tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to tab 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I think this needs a number, Your Honour, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 53, Your Honours, will be P1105.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: These are conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff from the 28th May, 1992. They were faxed, as indicated, to Bosanski Novi and Sanski Most. And if you could look quickly at conclusion number 7, it states: "If they want to move from the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the members of the Muslim and Croatian nationality, or the SDA and HDZ parties, together with representatives of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, must provide the endangered Serbian people, subjects of an unfathomable genocide, collective evacuation to their settlements, that is, a reciprocal exchange must be provided." And then if I could ask you to also look quickly at a related decision that's from the next day, May 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That needs to be distributed, Your Honour, although it is a previous exhibit, P64A, binder 18, footnote 372 [Realtime transcript read in error "72"].

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In conclusion 1 of this -- of the meeting held on 29 May 1992, it focuses on the same issue in conclusion 1, indicating that: "It has been decided that all Muslims and Croats, who so wish, should be able to move out of the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, but on condition that Serbs living outside of the Serbian autonomous districts and regions are allowed to move into the territories of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Autonomous Region of Krajina. In this manner, an exchange of population or, more precisely, a re-settlement of people from one part of the former SR BiH to another would be carried out in an organised manner." It goes on in the next paragraph to talk about the family-for-family principle, the concern of the ARK Crisis Staff with the fact that "several thousand Muslims from Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Bosanski Novi wish to move to Central Bosnia, of their own free will, whereas a great number of Serbs from Central Bosnia want to move to Krajina, but are not permitted by the local authorities, who are keeping them as some sort of hostage." And, Mr. Radojko, it's correct, isn't it, that that -- that those decisions were conveyed to the Petrovac municipality and discussed at a meeting held shortly afterward. And if you don't recall specifically, I can direct your attention to that specific Crisis Staff meeting.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like you to refer me to the meeting you have in mind. The decisions were delivered one way or the other; whether by facsimile or by someone who was actually physically going to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you'd turn to tab 54, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this is going to create confusion, but with respect to the previous exhibit, the transcript indicates P64A binder 18, footnote 72, it's footnote 372.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It had not confused me yet, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is P90, tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 54, Mr. Radojko, contains the minutes of the 24th Session of the Crisis Staff of the Petrovac municipality, held on the 2nd of June. And agenda item number 1 indicates as follows: "Bogdan Latinovic read the conclusions of the AR Krajina Crisis Staff in Banja Luka, reached at the session held on 29 May 1992. "After the discussion, the Crisis Staff of Petrovac Municipality gave a proposition for the aforementioned conclusions to be adopted in full, as follows ..." And as near as I can tell, it recites the language of the decision of 29 May. I won't read it again. There may be small distinctions, but I think that's essentially the thrust of that agenda item. And that would represent a correct chronology of events regarding that particular ARK conclusion, its dissemination, and adoption. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness needs to read the whole of number 1. It's not -- goes on, is not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like to read the whole of the first portion, Mr. Radojko? Then you have an opportunity to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's no need for that. Whilst they were talking, I kind of scanned the text. It is not about the adoption of any conclusions, it is about receiving information. The lady who was in charge of the minutes made a mistake, that was all. According -- because according to a logical approach, they couldn't adopt these conclusions because they had already been adopted, so they simply took note of the conclusions in question. They were a level below, so they couldn't either argue with this or confirm it in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could they have said, "We do not wish to do this"? I mean, it sounds as if whatever comes from above is accepted as ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall what they actually discussed on that occasion, although, as I can see, I have attended. I seem to have attended this meeting. They simply, presumably, went through this in a formal fashion, listened to this, and then left, because I can see that -- well, in fact, it was a rather lengthy meeting, an hour and a half. I can't remember, but it can't be a matter of them adopting anything of the sort. They could only take note of it, take note of the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, the last lines of paragraph 1 read: "The Crisis Staff has invited the leaderships of the SDA and the HDZ to actively take part in enabling the evacuation of the population." So that doesn't sound that much of just taking note of what has been decided elsewhere, but looks, rather, as an active attempt to implement what -- what has been decided.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that it looks that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but could you please be -- Mr. Radojko, I'm asking you this question and I'm -- when we look at this document, you have explained to us in length that you were only meeting the desire of all the Muslims to leave; that was what you intended to do. If seven municipalities produce a document in which we -- they say: Let's get the number of non-Serbs down to a level which suits us, and if this document says that of course they can leave if we get, in return, Serbs for it, so this document does not give a similar impression as you gave us in your answers. It is a document which tells us: They want to leave, fine, but only if we get Serbs in return for that. That's a totally different story, just as is the seven municipalities documents a totally different story from what you've told us. And I'm seeking a -- well, you say it -- we passively took note of it. And of course Mr. Tieger has -- as you said, that these kind of things later actually did happen to some extent. Could you explain this difference in what you tell us and what we read in these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must stress that quite a bit of what I've said was actually my own interpretation in an attempt to reconstruct a number of events on the basis of what I see in front of me. It is rather difficult for me to pre-empt other people's intentions. I'm simply telling you what I remember. For example, at those meetings here, the conclusions were not developed and drafted on that occasion, and the document that we have here refers to a decision of the AR Krajina. And according to the nature of events, they couldn't adopt it but they could take note of it and move on to implement it actively. Perhaps that's what it is about, that they agreed that they will implement the decision. But as to exchanges of population, I don't know what exactly they had in mind and who participated in those negotiations. I was not even in a position to attend meetings of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Radojko, you were perfectly able to explain all the reasons behind accommodating the wishes of the non-Serbs, which of course you agreed that circumstances were very difficult for them, but it was all about "That's what they wished and we just helped them to achieve that where we could not perhaps achieve what would have been best for all of us, that is that there would be no violence by gangs, et cetera," but very much a helpful and positive approach. Whatever piece of paper we read, it's totally different. What makes you believe -- and that's what I'm seeking: What makes you perceive this whole situation as an ultimate attempt to assist non-Serbs whereas every piece of paper -- well, of course not every, this is an exaggeration, but many of these documents give a totally different picture, that is: We want to have them below a certain number, we will let them go if at least we get in return Serbs for them, and perhaps other examples to follow. How could it be that you perceived the matter, in your position, so differently from the impression that's given in these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand what the problem is. I regret that there seems to be a misunderstanding here. When I talk about events, I only refer to the municipality in which I lived and on behalf of whose administration I did the job I did. I would like to stress that the understanding is due to the fact that we were an isolated case down there. That municipality was a unique one. In that municipality, first of all, Muslims were in a minority, and I said that my view was that they posed no serious threat to Serbs, even with all the weapons that they had managed to obtain. Secondly, they found themselves on a very small territory, almost like a ghetto. I myself had the impression that the overwhelming majority of that population were not militants, felt no animosity, and the most extreme ones had either already been spotted or had already fled the area. And I'm sorry that there seems to be an impression that I said about all of them, that they wished to leave. I was talking about the largest group, and there it was my clear impression that they left because of this pressure of -- because of those events, because I could see people begging to be allowed to leave. In a previous period of time, they might have wanted to. Something else --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you say: "I could see people begging to be allowed to leave," and at the same time I see a document in which it said: One family for one family, which does not give the impression that if they begged to leave, that you said: Okay, please go. You say it's one family for one family. And this same document says the Crisis Staff has decided to form a board for the implementation of these conclusions, that is, on the evacuation of Muslims from the territory of Petrovac municipality. It doesn't say let's try to see whether we can protect them in the best way we can and if they really want to leave, let's not apply a one-family-for-one-family approach, let's -- I'm puzzled by the differences between the paperwork and the testimony you are giving.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. There is, and I'm aware of it throughout. I'm referring to you what actually happened, not what was put down in writing. This principle, one family for one family, as far as I can remember was never even mentioned for real. It might have been in this text that came from Banja Luka and that was the end of it. Because it was not possible, under the circumstances, Your Honour. Serbs, refugees from Bihac, had already crossed over to the Serb side, most of them; about 4 to 5.000 of them had already moved to the area of Petrovac municipality. So if we had applied this principle, it would have been totally impossible to implement, and a whole range of these points here simply make no sense. I'm telling you what actually happened and not what they put down in writing. Whoever speaks Serbian can see that there is not even any syntax to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then, Mr. Radojko, I would expect the minutes or reports or meetings to say: Well, this is the -- these were the conclusions they reached, but it's all totally irrelevant for us because there's no reason for us to do anything like that. But the document says something totally different. It says: We're creating a board which will implement or -- which does not match with your explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My interpretation is -- does not run counter to the fact that the commission was set up. It was indeed set up, as you can see. Or, rather, whether it was actually operational, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least if you set up such a board, it's usually done with the intention to make it operational, even if it fails to become operational at that time. If on from the beginning you don't want such a board to become operational, there's no need to create it, would there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, but I can't remember it being operational. Most of these people are still alive and they can tell you themselves. I suppose they never did anything at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who were the members of this board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it follows from this, they were Hidic Safet, who was a member of the Assembly on behalf of the SDA Party; then Refik Bahtirjarevic, who was a businessman; then Dragan Ivanic, who was the president of the Serb Democratic Party; and Slavko Banjac was an employee in a state-owned company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were they all Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Two were Muslims and two Serbs. Hidic and Bahtirjarevic were Muslims, and Ivanic and Banjac were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock. Would this be a suitable time to have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll first ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I am aware that the Chamber took some of the time. Yes. Your expression of your face is telling us that you would certainly agree with us. How much time would you still need, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll do my best to go over the material. I think I probably need -- well, depending on how we go, because it may, again, be material that sparks some inquiry by the Chamber, but I'm estimating an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's a response the Chamber could expect, that it also depends --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not trying to discourage the Court's inquiry - I understand it - I just want -- accept it and it has to be calculated in accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to -- because, Mr. Josse, you need some considerable time as well, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm planning a lengthy re-examination, taking up the offer of the Chamber to do exactly that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's only fair, yes. We'll have a break now for 25 minutes, but how much time would you guess you would need, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: An hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: An hour and a half. Then, Mr. Tieger, you're invited to see -- I'm not counting the time taken by the Chamber, to finish in 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will indicate to the Court I will spend the recess doing my best to pare it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I wish to address the issue of P1104 at some stage. It was an insinuation, it was a suggestion by me that my learned friend's cross-examination was unfair in relation to that document, and I wish to make that clear at some juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not necessarily at this very moment. We'll then adjourn and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, did I understand well that you would like to raise a procedural issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. It's a very short matter, but, Your Honour, it relates to -- well, Your Honour, would you forgive me for a moment, because following yesterday I'm just checking something. Your Honour, it relates to a witness, but it's a matter of a fairly personal nature, Your Honour, and it would require very, very brief closed session so that I can just say what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We turn into closed session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Madam Usher, could you try and see whether the witness could again be brought to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Radojko. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, please turn to tab 42. The minutes of the 45th Session of the Board of Commissioners - maybe I'll check the original on that - held on 31 July 1992, and I'd like you to look specifically at the decision under agenda item 2. Top of the page of the English at page 2, and it begins with the words: "Rajko Novakovic, Dragan Milanovic, Drago Gacesa discussed the questions asked. Following the discussion, the Board of Commissioners adopted a Decision to appoint a commission for the departure of Muslims. Those appointed to the commission are: Jovica Sepa, Dragan Gacesa, Obrad Vrzina, Jovo Radojko and Dragan Ivanic. "The commission will establish who can leave the Petrovac Municipality and the condition will be for them to exchange their property or to give it to the state, that is, to the Serbian Municipality of Petrovac; those who have such a certificate will de-register themselves at the public security station and will be able to leave the Petrovac public security area in an organised manner." That's the commission you were referring to earlier, Mr. Radojko?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet, or maybe I'm looking at the wrong document, but I recall this from my earlier testimony. That's 42, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct --

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 42, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct. It's a meeting that was held on 31 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it now. Undoubtedly the members of the commission are listed here. That's the commission I was appointed to whilst I was on the front line, but I know that the commission never met and never did anything. At least, I took no part in it and I suppose they would have invited me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look --

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I've found this section. Sepa, Gacesa, Vrzina; five of them in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And Vrzina's the military representative of the Crisis Staff, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Gacesa the police representative?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sepa, his position?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sepa was the chief of municipal general administration. He was the head of the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ivanic, was he the president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe that he was at the time. Yes, actually, I'm certain of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look next, please, at tab 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the way, Your Honour, for the record tab 42 was P90, tab 39. P41 needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P41, Mr. Radojko, is a statement by the president of the commission, Obrad Vrzina, stating that: "Pursuant to decision number -" and it's listed - "of the War Presidency dated 31 July 1992, Muslims may move away voluntarily on the following conditions: 1. If they sign a contract on the exchange of immovable property. 2. If they sign a statement giving their immovable property to the state." And then the last sentence of the next paragraph indicates that: "Immovable property may be given to close relatives from mixed marriages." So that was an act by the president of the commission which was responding to the decision of the War Presidency on 31 July 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's absolutely right. And when you say -- and what you say, an act by the president, of course means that he probably drafted this himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And now I would like to turn quickly to tabs 44 and 45 and look at the couple of records and ask you if those are records of people attempting to fulfil the conditions established by the commission for moving out pursuant to the decision of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab -- I think these both need numbers -- I'm sorry, 44 is P90, tab 40, and both of them are located at that tab, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So P44 indicates a record that is signed by Samir Hodzic. P45 indicates a record signed by Smajlo Mumicehajic. Both of those, Mr. Radojko, indicate a declaration that the undersigned declares in his name with regard to specified residential property, et cetera, that: "I concede it permanently to the Petrovac Municipal Assembly. "I have made this declaration with full responsibility, without coercion and in full consciousness of my declaration, for the purpose of obtaining the necessary documentation for permanent departure from and leaving Petrovac municipality." These are in fact the documents that were required pursuant to the conditions that we looked at just a moment ago, enabling Muslims to de-register and leave Petrovac municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll ask you this question because I think the Court may ask it if I don't: You talked a great deal about the efforts of the municipality to take care of the Muslims' property and anticipate their return. This document indicates that these people are obliged, in order to leave the municipality, to sign it over permanently to the Petrovac municipality in order to obtain their permanent departure, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was giving you my understanding of the events and what the legal situation was. I've already seen such type of documents as we can see under 41. Even before they started filling these forms out, I told them that this was null and void and that, indeed, such a document could never be valid, under no circumstances. Very few of these were produced, in fact, because they realised that it was pointless. Formally speaking, you are right, but I was already referring to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I have some problems in 44, 45. What appears on 45 in English is certainly not a translation of what I find in B/C/S under 45. Let me just check with my colleagues. Yes, that's true for everyone as far as I can see. What I find in the original is at least a list of six persons and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's -- as you can see, let me interrupt, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you can see from 44, it was an obvious -- what appears to be -- to correspond precisely to the English translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 44's fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But 45 we find approximately a similar translation into English, but a -- 10th of August -- yes. It very much looks like the English version of 44, although it's a bit different, no handwriting on it in the translation. But most of it the same. But the original is something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And I -- as you -- the Court may see also that these are -- I think these documents were submitted sequentially, so the translation ERN is 03009090 for 44; for 45 it's 9091.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I think, unfortunately, the B/C/S document here simply doesn't correspond, but we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- can provide it. I don't think it creates any problem at this point since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't create a huge problem, but of course I would like to know what actually the document is under 45, where it seems not to be what the English translation says it is. Totally different documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. If you could try to find the good one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And thank you for that, Your Honour. I will attend to it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, if you could turn to tab 49, please. This is a 21 October proposal on the distribution -- the way of the war booty distribution pursuant to the decision of the War Presidency of Petrovac municipality. It indicates resigning commission president Jovo Radojko --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This needs a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1101 [sic], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I don't want to spend time on this, Mr. Radojko, at least not unnecessary time. Is it correct that, at least for a period of time, you were the commission president of the Petrovac municipality commission for the collection and distribution of war booty and booties gained in other ways?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed to that duty and, as you were able to see, I resigned pretty soon. But they never accepted my resignation. I even asked for my resignation to be accepted in writing on several occasions, and each time they refused to. There was a decree number 899 -- from 1992, which was published in the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska, issue number 8, wherein the commission was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, the booty referred to is exclusively, or at least primarily, property that had once been owned by Muslims. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of my appointment, different matters were involved, but most often they were vehicles brought over from the war-affected areas. I suppose that these were items leftover by the Muslims in the area. This area was north-west of -- the north-western part of Bihac municipality. Later on they collected the livestock that was left behind by the Muslims who left Petrovac, and they stationed themselves on a farm there. As this was done arbitrarily, I resigned because I refused to continue doing things and signing things I thought were unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You said -- for 44 and 45, let's go back to 44 and 45. If you could go back to 44 and 45.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have gone to that tab, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to get your reaction to these forms that were drafted. You told us: [In English] "Even before filling these forms out, I told them that this was null and void and that, indeed, such a document could never be valid, under no such circumstances." [Interpretation] So apart from the fact that this document is valid or not valid or that it would have a legal value or not, what's your feeling about the fact that even people had the idea of coming up with this kind of document? What's your reaction when you see this kind of document? I'm not talking about the legal aspect of things, but what do you think about this? What's your feeling behind this? The legal analysis that you make is maybe interesting, but what's your gut feeling? What was your gut feeling when you knew about these forms? And now that we tell you about these forms, what's the gut feeling that you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After all the things that happened, my reaction is much milder than it was at the time. This type of form under 45 I was able to see back in time when Milka Jevic, head of administration, showed it to me. I knew that they had developed a document and I wanted to read it. I told everyone I met that this was nonsense, pointless, and idiotic. As the events unfolded, this proved to be pointless and unnecessary. I don't know what happened at the end of the day, but I know that people stopped showing up to sign such records. I know that very few such statements were, in fact, signed compared to the numbers that could have been made. My reaction was quite sharp. Now, what would I say to that today? Well, we have had a legal system in place for at least 2.000 years. I have some family experience in connection with this, and I knew that sooner or later this was going to be revoked in legal terms and that this was untenable. It simply served to produce a further negative image of the people. When I look at the document, I see something that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a technical problem with microphones with the French booth, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's working again, Mr. Chairman, it's working again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now get a message that the problem has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wonder what was lost. I asked Judge Hanoteau whether he was listening to the French channel, but he was listening to the English channel. Could the interpreters give us an impression on where they may have had these problems?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth encountered no problems, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's gone off again. I understand. It's not the English booth. The French booth has the problem and whenever you have the problem it starts ticking in my earphones. Is it working again? I'm now addressing the French booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I receive no answer on the French channel, so it's -- the technicians are going to assist us. I will switch to the French channel and see whether it's not yet resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're asked to have a break of ten minutes to fix the issue, but I would then prefer to have a break until a quarter past 5.00 and then continue until 7.00 once we've returned. I'm afraid -- otherwise we would need two breaks and that usually takes more time. We'll, for technical reasons, have an early second break and we'll resume at quarter past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, you made mention before the break of your concern over the negative image that might result from the certificates we looked at. In fact, pursuant to the instructions of President Novakovic, you were the person in charge of contact with the media, generally speaking, weren't you? And here I'm quoting from your testimony in the Brdjanin case from page 20196.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My channel was at 0 when I re-entered the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to be okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, could you please repeat your question so that Mr. Radojko can hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, you made mention before the break of your concern over the negative image that might result from the certificates we reviewed. In fact, pursuant to the instructions of President Novakovic, you were the person in charge of contact with the media, generally speaking, weren't you? And here I'm quoting from your testimony in the Brdjanin case from page 20196. Did you hear the question, Mr. Radojko?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I was just expecting you to continue. But I was not worried about the image, I was worried about the possible consequences arising from this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, sorry. I apologise to -- the question is: You were the person in charge of contact with the media, generally speaking. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, to a certain extent, except in case the president changed his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection, let me direct your attention quickly to a couple of entries in your diary; first the August 10th entry, English at 129, B/C/S at 118. That's tab 4. This is a matter, Mr. Radojko, you testified about during the Brdjanin case and it's translated here as: "Announcement: The Balic family was killed by Muslim extremists ... "A propaganda campaign is underway for all Muslims to move out, which is unacceptable." And it was discussed during the course of the Brdjanin case as a press release, so I take it that's what's meant by "announcement." Did you find that entry, sir? Okay. So is it correct you were tasked to issue a press release that the Balic family was killed by Muslim extremists and to say that a propaganda campaign is underway for all Muslims to move out, which is unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's totally wrong. I don't see how you're establishing a link between myself and the press communique.
